jones_tonetti.authors: Charles I. Jones and Christopher Tonetti
jones_tonetti.title: Past Automation and Future A.I.: How Weak Links Tame the Growth Explosion
jones_tonetti.locations: Introduction, printed pp. 2–3; Figure 5 and discussion, printed pp. 40–41.
jones_tonetti.mechanism: Automation of production and of idea production creates a feedback loop. Strong task complementarity makes the remaining essential labor tasks bottlenecks. Aggregate acceleration depends on assumptions about how broadly rapid machine-productivity improvements spread.

historical_continuation_calibration.object: Growth of output per person, not total GDP growth or a cumulative level gain. Historical private-business calibration.

jones_tonetti.alternative_calibration: Moore's Law Everywhere uses much faster machine-productivity growth calibrated to the computer sector and yields much faster aggregate acceleration. It is an assumption-driven alternative, not an observed forecast.
jones_tonetti.classroom_example: Perfect-complements teaching illustration, not an empirical estimate: one left and one right shoe are required for each pair. Hold left-shoe capacity at 100 per day. Raising right-shoe capacity from 100 to arbitrarily large output leaves pair output at 100. This holds the left-shoe capacity fixed; labor reallocation or investment in that capacity can raise output.

three_scenarios.source: Figure 5a (capital share) and 5b (growth), printed p. 40 / zero-indexed PDF page 40; discussion pp. 39--43.
three_scenarios.calibration: AI as a continuation of historical private-business patterns; not the faster Moore's Law Everywhere calibration of Figure 6.
three_scenarios.units: Annual growth of output per person, percent; labour income as percent of total factor income. Both are model simulations, not observations or forecasts.

definitions.full: All tasks automated in finite time.
definitions.asymptotic: Automated task share tends to 100 percent without reaching it in finite time; the paper labels this Baseline.
definitions.partial: A positive set of essential tasks is never automated.

long_run.asymptotic: Positive finite balanced-growth rate in this historical calibration; not a universal result for asymptotic automation.
long_run.partial: Growth ultimately limited by human-task productivity, 0.5 percent per year in the calibration.

three_scenarios.transformation: Recover annual vertices of all three scenarios in both panels. x=112/782 maps to 2020/2160. y=427/36 maps to 0/20 percent in growth and 0/100 percent in capital share. Compute labour share as 100 minus the capital-share percentage, consistent with s_L = 1 - s_K in this model. Join scenario/year one-to-one. No simulation re-estimation, smoothing, interpolation, or extrapolation. Omit the separate constant-growth reference line.
three_scenarios.labor_share_interpretation: A share of factor income, not the share of employed workers, a wage level, or a prediction that individual earnings change in the same direction. Full automation tends to zero labour share; partial automation tends to 100 percent; the asymptotic baseline tends to roughly 64 percent in this calibration.
three_scenarios.precision: Approximate values recovered from the published figure; six decimals preserve its geometry, not economic precision.
three_scenarios.short_run: Figure 5 and its discussion describe nearly indistinguishable paths for approximately the next 50 years. The shaded 2020--2070 interval highlights this comparison, not a predicted structural break.
three_scenarios.mechanism: Strong complementarity means remaining essential human tasks constrain aggregate production. Automation of goods and ideas accelerates growth, but weak links delay the acceleration.

anthropic_scenarios.authors: Anton Korinek, Charles I. Jones, Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter and Peter McCrory
anthropic_scenarios.title: Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI
anthropic_scenarios.location: Table 3, printed p. 31 / zero-indexed PDF page 30; rows GDP growth and Labor share, verified against the original table.
anthropic_scenarios.timing: Beginning of 2030. GDP growth rates are log changes over the preceding 12 months, not cumulative gains to 2030. Labor share is labor income as a percentage of total income.
anthropic_scenarios.scope: US economy, conditional model scenarios determined by AI capabilities, diffusion, automation versus augmentation, productivity gains, new tasks and worker reallocation frictions. Neither assigned probabilities nor asserted most-likely forecasts.

sequence: Left/right shoe complementarity and bottleneck example
Three Jones--Tonetti automation scenarios: similar short run, divergent long run
classroom_presentation.jones_tonetti_scope: Figure 5a--b historical calibration: paired growth and labour-share panels with common years and scenario colours. Labour share is one minus the published capital share. The asymptotic case is the published Baseline.
classroom_presentation.anthropic_scope: Removed from slide 69; verified values retained only as source history.
classroom_presentation.baumol_scope: Existing Statistics Canada price chart shown as a full-slide figure without changing data. Quartet intuition and the AI-growth link remain in the source for oral exposition. Relative-price differences have causes other than productivity; the chart does not identify a causal Baumol effect.

solow_quote.author: Robert M. Solow
solow_quote.quote: You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.
solow_quote.title: We’d Better Watch Out
solow_quote.publication: The New York Times Book Review
solow_quote.verification: Read the original scanned review: quotation in the middle column, date and page number at the bottom. The displayed quotation uses the original English wording.
solow_quote.classroom_design: 1987 quotation paired with 2026 firm survey evidence. Survey responses are not a causal estimate of aggregate productivity growth.
